entries.b9e46edff9f48e03a6b8580e0dfb70001cc98102: <div sID="gen4905" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Judg.12" sID="Judg.12"/> <div eID="gen4905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4906" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4907" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. Jephthah's rencounter with the Ephraimites, and the blood shed on that unhappy occasion (<reference osisRef="Judg.12.1-Judg.12.6">ver. 1-6</reference>), and the conclusion of Jephthah's life and government, <reference osisRef="Judg.12.7">ver. 7</reference>. II. A short account of three other of the judges of Israel: Ibzan (<reference osisRef="Judg.12.8-Judg.12.10">ver. 8-10</reference>), Elon (<reference osisRef="Judg.12.11-Judg.12.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>), Abdon, <reference osisRef="Judg.12.13-Judg.12.15">ver. 13-15</reference>.
entries.7101af70f6716d4a1e507284101938bc3d8a39bb: <div eID="gen4907" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4906" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Displeasure of the Ephraimites; Punishment of the Ephraimites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1143.)</title> <div sID="gen4908" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the men of Ephraim gathered themselves together, and went northward, and said unto Jephthah, Wherefore passedst thou over to fight against the children of Ammon, and didst not call us to go with thee? we will burn thine house upon thee with fire. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Jephthah said unto them, I and my people were at great strife with the children of Ammon; and when I called you, ye delivered me not out of their hands. <hi type="super">3</hi> And when I saw that ye delivered <hi type="italic">me</hi> not, I put my life in my hands, and passed over against the children of Ammon, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> delivered them into my hand: wherefore then are ye come up unto me this day, to fight against me? <hi type="super">4</hi> Then Jephthah gathered together all the men of Gilead, and fought with Ephraim: and the men of Gilead smote Ephraim, because they said, Ye Gileadites <hi type="italic">are</hi> fugitives of Ephraim among the Ephraimites, <hi type="italic">and</hi> among the Manassites. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the Gileadites took the passages of Jordan before the Ephraimites: and it was <hi type="italic">so,</hi> that when those Ephraimites which were escaped said, Let me go over; that the men of Gilead said unto him, <hi type="italic">Art</hi> thou an Ephraimite? If he said, Nay; <hi type="super">6</hi> Then said they unto him, Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth: for he could not frame to pronounce <hi type="italic">it</hi> right. Then they took him, and slew him at the passages of Jordan: and there fell at that time of the Ephraimites forty and two thousand. <hi type="super">7</hi> And Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then died Jephthah the Gileadite, and was buried in <hi type="italic">one of</hi> the cities of Gilead. <div eID="gen4908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4909" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The unreasonable displeasure of the men of Ephraim against Jephthah, because he had not called them in to his assistance against the Ammonites, that they might share in the triumphs and spoils, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.1">v. 1</reference>. Pride was at the bottom of the quarrel. Only by that comes contention. Proud men think all the honours lost that go beside themselves, and then <hi type="italic">who can stand before envy?</hi> The Ephraimites had the same quarrel with Gideon (<reference osisRef="Judg.8.1">ch. viii. 1</reference>), who was of Manasseh on their side Jordan, as Jephthah was of Manasseh on the other side Jordan. Ephraim and Manasseh were hearer akin than any other of the tribes, being both the sons of Joseph, and yet they were more jealous one of another than any other of the tribes. Jacob having crossed hands, and given Ephraim the preference, looking as far forward as the kingdom of the ten tribes, which Ephraim was the head of, after the revolt from the house of David, that tribe, not content with that honour in the promise, was displeased if Manasseh had any honour done it in the mean time. It is a pity that kindred or relationship, which should be an inducement to love and peace, should be ever an occasion (as it often proves) of strife and discord. <hi type="italic">A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city, and contentions among brethren are as the bars of a castle.</hi> The anger of the Ephraimites at Jephthah was, 1. Causeless and unjust. Why <hi type="italic">didst thou not call us to go with thee?</hi> For a good reason. Because it was the men of Gilead that had made him their captain, not the men of Ephraim, so that he had no authority to call them. Had his attempt miscarried for want of their help, they might justly have blamed him for not desiring it. But when the work was done, and done effectually, the Ammonites being subdued and Israel delivered, there was no harm done, though their hands were not employed in it. 2. It was cruel and outrageous. They get together in a tumultuous manner, pass over Jordan as far as Mizpeh in Gilead, where Jephthah lived, and no less will satisfy their fury but they will burn his house and him in it. <hi type="italic">Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce.</hi> Those resentments that have the least reason for them have commonly the most rage in them. Jephthah was now a conqueror over the common enemies of Israel, and they should have come to congratulate him, and return him the thanks of their tribe for the good services he had done; but we must not think it strange if we receive ill from those from whom we deserve well. Jephthah was now a mourner for the calamity of his family upon his daughter's account, and they should have come to condole with him and comfort him; but barbarous men take a pleasure in adding affliction to the afflicted. In this world, the end of one trouble often proves the beginning of another; nor must we ever <hi type="italic">boast as though we had put off the harness.</hi> <div eID="gen4909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4910" type="x-p"/> II. Jephthah's warm vindication of himself. He did not endeavour to pacify them, as Gideon had done in the like case; the Ephraimites were now more outrageous than they were them, and Jephthah had not so much of a meek and quiet spirit as Gideon had. Whether they would be pacified or no, Jephthah takes care, <div eID="gen4910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4911" type="x-p"/> 1. To justify himself, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.2-Judg.11.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. He makes it out that they had no cause at all to quarrel with him, for, (1.) It was not in pursuit of glory that he had engaged in this war, but for the necessary defence of his country, with which the children of Ammon greatly strove. (2.) He had invited the Ephraimites to come and join with him, though he neither needed them nor was under any obligation to pay that respect to them, but they had declined the service: <hi type="italic">I called you, and you delivered me not out of their hands.</hi> Had that been true which they charged him with, yet it would not have been a just ground of quarrel; but it seems it was false, and, as the matter of fact now appears, he had more cause to quarrel with them for deserting the common interests of Israel in a time of need. It is no new thing for those who are themselves most culpable to be most clamorous in accusing the innocent. (3.) The enterprise was very hazardous, and they had more reason to pity him than to be angry with him: <hi type="italic">I put my life in my hands,</hi> that is, "exposed myself to the utmost peril in what I did, having so small an army," The honour they envied was bought dearly enough; they needed not to grudge it to him; few of them would have ventured so far for it. (4.) He does not take the glory of the success to himself (that would have been invidious), but gives it all to God: "<hi type="italic">The Lord delivered them into my hands.</hi> If God was pleased so far to make use of me for his glory, why should you be offended at that? Have you any reason to <hi type="italic">fight against me?</hi> Is not that in effect to fight against God, in whose hand I have been only an unworthy instrument?" <div eID="gen4911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4912" type="x-p"/> 2. When this just answer (though not so soft an answer as Gideon's) did not prevail to turn away their wrath, he took care both to defend himself from their fury and to chastise their insolence with the sword, by virtue of his authority as Israel's judge. (1.) The Ephraimites had not only quarrelled with Jephthah, but, when his neighbours and friends appeared to take his part, they had abused them, and given them foul language; for I adhere to our translation, and so take it, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.4">v. 4</reference>. They said in scorn, "You Gileadites that dwell here on the other side Jordan are but fugitives of Ephraim, the scum and dregs of the tribes of Joseph, of which Ephraim is the chief, the refuse of the family, and are so accounted among the Ephraimites and among the Manassites. Who cares for you? All your neighbours know what you are, no better than fugitives and vagabonds, separated from your brethren, and driven hither into a corner." The Gileadites were as true Israelites as any other, and at this time had signalized themselves, both in the choice of Jephthah and in the war with Ammon, above all the families of Israel, and yet are most basely and unjustly called <hi type="italic">fugitives.</hi> It is an ill thing to fasten names or characters of reproach upon persons or countries, as is common, especially upon those that lie under outward disadvantages: it often occasions quarrels that prove of ill consequence, as it did here. See likewise what a mischievous thing an abusive tongue is, that calls ill names, and gives scurrilous language: it <hi type="italic">sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire of hell</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.3.6">Jam. iii. 6</reference>), and many a time cuts the throat of him that uses it, as it did here, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.8">Ps. lxiv. 8</reference>. If these Ephraimites could have denied themselves the poor satisfaction of calling the Gileadites <hi type="italic">fugitives,</hi> they might have prevented a great deal of bloodshed; for <hi type="italic">grievous words stir up anger,</hi> and who knows how great a matter a little of that fire may kindle? (2.) This affront raises the Gileadites' blood, and the indignity done to themselves, as well as to their captain, must be revenged. [1.] They routed them in the field, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.4">v. 4</reference>. They fought with Ephraim, and, Ephraim being but a rude unheaded rabble, smote Ephraim, and put them to flight. [2.] They cut off their retreat, and so completed their revenge, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.5-Judg.11.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. The Gileadites, who perhaps were better acquainted with the passages of Jordan than the Ephraimites were, secured them with strong guards, who were ordered to slay every Ephraimite that offered to pass the river. Here was, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Cruelty enough in the destruction of them. Sufficient surely was <hi type="italic">the punishment which was inflicted by many;</hi> when they were routed in the field, there needed not this severity to cut off all that escaped. Shall the sword devour for ever? Whether Jephthah is to be praised for this I know not; perhaps he saw it to be a piece of necessary justice. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Cunning enough in the discovery of them. It seems the Ephraimites, though they spoke the same language with other Israelites, yet had got a custom in the dialect of their country to pronounce the Hebrew letter <hi type="italic">Shin</hi> like <hi type="italic">Samech,</hi> and they had so strangely used themselves to it that they could not do otherwise, no, not to save their lives. We learn to speak by imitation; those that first used <hi type="italic">s</hi> for <hi type="italic">sh,</hi> did it either because it was shorter or because it was finer, and their children learnt to speak like them, so that you might know an Ephraimite by it; as in England we know a west-country man or a north-country man, nay, perhaps a Shropshire man, and a Cheshire man, by his pronunciation. <hi type="italic">Thou art a Galilean, and thy speech betrays thee.</hi> By this the Ephraimites were discovered. If they took a man that they suspected to be an Ephraimite, but he denied it, they bade him say <hi type="italic">Shibboleth;</hi> but either he <hi type="italic">could not,</hi> as our translation reads it, or he did not heed, or frame, or direct himself, as some read, to pronounce it aright, but said <hi type="italic">Sibboleth,</hi> and so was known to be an Ephraimite, and was slain immediately. <hi type="italic">Shibboleth</hi> signifies a <hi type="italic">river or stream:</hi> "Ask leave to go over Shibboleth, the river." Those that were thus cut off made up the whole number of slaughtered Ephraimites forty-two thousand, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.6">v. 6</reference>. Thus another mutiny of that angry tribe was prevented. <div eID="gen4912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4913" type="x-p"/> 3. Now let us observe the righteousness of God in the punishment of these proud and passionate Ephraimites, which in several instances answered to their sin. (1.) They were proud of the honour of their tribe, gloried in this, that they were Ephraimites; but how soon were they brought to be ashamed or afraid to own their country! <hi type="italic">Art thou an Ephraimite?</hi> No, now rather of any tribe than that. (2.) They had gone in a rage over Jordan to burn Jephthah's house with fire, but now they came back to Jordan as sneakingly as they had passed it furiously, and were cut off from ever returning to their own houses. (3.) They had upbraided the Gileadites with the infelicity of their country, lying at such a distance, and now they suffered by an infirmity peculiar to their own country, in not being able to pronounce <hi type="italic">Shibboleth.</hi> (4.) They had called the Gileadites, unjustly, fugitives, and now they really and in good earnest became fugitives themselves; and in the Hebrew the same word (<reference osisRef="Judg.11.5">v. 5</reference>) is used of the Ephraimites that escaped, or that fled, which they had used in scorn of the Gileadites, calling them <hi type="italic">fugitives.</hi> He that rolls the stone of reproach unjustly upon another, let him expect that it will justly return upon himself. <div eID="gen4913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4914" type="x-p"/> III. Here is the end of Jephthah's government. He judged Israel but six years, and then died, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.7">v. 7</reference>. Perhaps the death of his daughter sunk him so that he never looked up afterwards, but it shortened his days, and he went to his grave mourning.
entries.64b978cf27c9c3b04d1a95c8f005dd8ef2c9c0a8: <div eID="gen4914" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jephthah's Successors. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1112.)</title> <div sID="gen4915" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And after him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he had thirty sons, and thirty daughters, <hi type="italic">whom</hi> he sent abroad, and took in thirty daughters from abroad for his sons. And he judged Israel seven years. <hi type="super">10</hi> Then died Ibzan, and was buried at Bethlehem. <hi type="super">11</hi> And after him Elon, a Zebulonite, judged Israel; and he judged Israel ten years. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Elon the Zebulonite died, and was buried in Aijalon in the country of Zebulun. <hi type="super">13</hi> And after him Abdon the son of Hillel, a Pirathonite, judged Israel. <hi type="super">14</hi> And he had forty sons and thirty nephews, that rode on threescore and ten ass colts: and he judged Israel eight years. <hi type="super">15</hi> And Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite died, and was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the mount of the Amalekites. <div eID="gen4915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4916" type="x-p"/> We have here a short account of the short reigns of three more of the judges of Israel, the first of whom governed but seven years, the second ten, and the third eight. <hi type="italic">For the transgression of a land, many are the princes thereof,</hi> many in a short time, successively (<reference osisRef="Prov.28.2">Prov. xxviii. 2</reference>), good men being removed in the beginning of their usefulness and by the time that they have applied themselves to their business. <div eID="gen4916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4917" type="x-p"/> I. Ibzan of Bethlehem, most probably Bethlehem of Judah, David's city, not that in Zebulun, which is only mentioned once, <reference osisRef="Josh.19.15">Josh. xix. 15</reference>. He ruled but seven years, but by the number of his children, and his disposing of them all in marriage himself, it appears that he lived long; and probably the great increase of his family, and the numerous alliances he made, added to his personal merits, made him the more fit to be either chosen by the people as Jephthah was, or called of God immediately, as Gideon was, to be Israel's judge, to keep up and carry on the work of God among them. That which is remarkable concerning him is, 1. That he had many children, sixty in all, a quiver full of these arrows. Thus was Bethlehem of old famous for increase, the very city where <hi type="italic">he</hi> was to be born whose spiritual seed should be <hi type="italic">as the stars of heaven.</hi> 2. That he had an equal number of each sex, thirty sons and thirty daughters, a thing which does not often happen in the same family, yet, in the great family of mankind, he that at first made two, male and female, by his wise providence preserves a succession of both in some sort of equality as far as is requisite to the keeping up of the generations of men upon earth. 3. That he took care to marry them all. His daughters he sent abroad, <hi type="italic">et maritis dedit,</hi> so the vulgar Latin adds—<hi type="italic">he provided husbands for them;</hi> and, as it were in exchange, and both ways, strengthening his interest, he <hi type="italic">took in thirty daughters from abroad for his sons.</hi> The Jews say, Every father owes three things to his son: to teach him to read the law, give him a trade, and get him a wife. What a difference was there between Ibzan's family and that of his immediate predecessor Jephthah! Ibzan has sixty children and all married, Jephthah but one, a daughter, that dies or lives unmarried. Some are increased, others are diminished: both are the Lord's doing. <div eID="gen4917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4918" type="x-p"/> II. Elon of Zebulun, in the north of Canaan, was next raised up to preside in public affairs, to administer justice, and to reform abuses. Ten years he continued a blessing to Israel, and then died, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.11-Judg.11.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. Dr. Lightfoot computes that in the beginning of his time the forty years' oppression by the Philistines began (spoken of <reference osisRef="Judg.13.1">ch. xiii. 1</reference>), and about that time Samson was born. Probably, his residence being in the north, the Philistines who bordered upon the southern parts of Canaan took the opportunity of making incursions upon them. <div eID="gen4918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4919" type="x-p"/> III. Abdon, of the tribe of Ephraim, succeeded, and in him that illustrious tribe begins to recover its reputation, having not afforded any person of note since Joshua; for Abimelech the Shechemite was rather a scandal to it. This Abdon was famous for the multitude of his offspring (<reference osisRef="Judg.11.14">v. 14</reference>): he had forty sons and thirty grandsons, all of whom he lived to see grown up, and they rode on seventy ass-colts either as judges and officers or as gentlemen and persons of distinction. It was a satisfaction to him thus to see his children's children, but it is feared he did not see peace upon Israel, for by this time the Philistines had begun to break in upon them. Concerning this, and the rest of these judges that have ever so short an account given of them, yet notice is taken where they were buried (<reference osisRef="Judg.11.7">v. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.10">10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.12">12,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.15">15</reference>), perhaps because the inscriptions upon their monuments (for such were anciently used, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.17">2 Kings xxiii. 17</reference>) would serve for the confirmation and enlargement of their story, and might be consulted by such as desired further information concerning them. Peter, having occasion to speak of David, says, <hi type="italic">His sepulchre is with us unto this day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.29">Acts ii. 29</reference>. Or it is intended for the honour of the places where they laid their bones, but may be improved for the lessening of our esteem of all worldly glory, of which death and the grave will stain the pride. These judges, that were as gods to Israel, died like men, and all their honour was laid in the dust. <div eID="gen4919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4920" type="x-p"/> It is very strange that in the history of all these judges, some of whose actions are very particularly related, there is not so much as once mention made of the high priest, or any other priest or Levite, appearing either for counsel or action in any public affair, from Phinehas (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.28">Judg. xx. 28</reference>) to Eli, which may well be computed 250 years; only the names of the high priests at that time are preserved, <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.4-1Chr.6.7">1 Chron. vi. 4-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.35">and Ezra vii. 3-5</reference>. How can this strange obscurity of that priesthood for so long a time, now in the beginning of its days, agree with that mighty splendour with which it was introduced and the figure which the institution of it makes in the law of Moses? Surely it intimates that the institution was chiefly intended to be typical, and that the great benefits that seemed to be promised by it were to be chiefly looked for in its antitype, the everlasting priesthood of our Lord Jesus, in comparison of the superior glory of which that priesthood had no glory, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.10">2 Cor. iii. 10</reference>.  <chapter eID="Judg.12"/> <div eID="gen4920" type="x-p"/>

entries.3ed2ef5199a4594853f25ddd2ff851fd16d0ff66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2355"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.12.1-Judg.12.3">Jud 12:1-3</reference>. The Ephraimites Quarrelling with Jephthah.</title> <div sID="gen3172" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2355"/><hi type="bold">1. the men of Ephraim gathered themselves together--</hi>Hebrew, "were summoned."<div eID="gen3172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and went northward--</hi>After crossing the Jordan, their route from Ephraim was, strictly speaking, in a northeasterly direction, toward Mizpeh.<div eID="gen3173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3174" type="x-p"/> the men of Ephraim ... said unto Jephthah, Wherefore ... didst [thou] <hi type="bold">not call us?--</hi>This is a fresh development of the jealous, rash, and irritable temper of the Ephraimites. The ground of their offense now was their desire of enjoying the credit of patriotism although they had not shared in the glory of victory. <div eID="gen3174" type="x-p"/>
entries.e57964039fed94eece69c92607eea424172e3010: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2356"/><div sID="gen3175" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2356"/><hi type="bold">2. when I called you, ye delivered me not out of their hands--</hi>The straightforward answer of Jephthah shows that their charge was false; their complaint of not being treated as confederates and allies entirely without foundation; and their boast of a ready contribution of their services came with an ill grace from people who had purposely delayed appearing till the crisis was past. <div eID="gen3175" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d35fd5a3220589a64d9c60bb79b88b72fb4e8be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2357"/><div sID="gen3176" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2357"/><hi type="bold">3. when I saw that ye delivered me not, I put my life in my hands--</hi>A common form of speech in the East for undertaking a duty of imminent peril. This Jephthah had done, having encountered and routed the Ammonites with the aid of his Gileadite volunteers alone; and since the Lord had enabled him to conquer without requiring assistance from any other tribe, why should the Ephraimites take offense? They ought rather to have been delighted and thankful that the war had terminated without their incurring any labor and danger. <div eID="gen3176" type="x-p"/>
entries.52adb3f3061ebd01982d6bffb2e732a10e7ff6a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2358"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.12.4-Judg.12.15">Jud 12:4-15</reference>. Discerned by the Word Sibboleth, Are Slain by the Gileadites.</title> <div sID="gen3177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2358"/><hi type="bold">4-6. the men of Gilead smote Ephraim, because they said, Ye Gileadites are fugitives of Ephraim--</hi>The remonstrances of Jephthah, though reasonable and temperate, were not only ineffectual, but followed by insulting sneers that the Gileadites were reckoned both by the western Manassites and Ephraimites as outcasts--the scum and refuse of their common stock. This was addressed to a peculiarly sensitive people. A feud immediately ensued. The Gileadites, determined to chastise this public affront, gave them battle; and having defeated the Ephraimites, they chased their foul-mouthed but cowardly assailants out of the territory. Then rushing to the fords of the Jordan, they intercepted and slew every fugitive. The method adopted for discovering an Ephraimite was by the pronunciation of a word naturally suggested by the place where they stood. Shibboleth, means "a stream"; Sibboleth, "a burden." The Eastern tribe had, it seems, a dialectical provincialism in the sound of Shibboleth; and the Ephraimites could not bring their organs to pronounce it. <div eID="gen3177" type="x-p"/>
entries.d12d0a2109aec6087d94ffab5bedc6a228abd2cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2359"/><div sID="gen3178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2359"/><hi type="bold">7. Jephthah died--</hi>After a government of six years, this mighty man of valor died; and however difficult it may be for us to understand some passages in his history, he has been ranked by apostolic authority among the worthies of the ancient church. He was followed by a succession of minor judges, of whom the only memorials preserved relate to the number of their families and their state [Jud 12:8-15]. <chapter eID="Judg.12"/>

entries.03e867f54a2b3b23640c85432d839b64448e99c4: <div eID="gen8896" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen8897" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8898" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8898" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8897" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8899" type="x-p"/> The Ephraimites are incensed against Jephthah, because he did not call them to war against the Ammonites; and threaten his destruction, <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.1">Jdg 12:1</reference>. He vindicates himself, <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.2">Jdg 12:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.3">Jdg 12:3</reference>; and arms the Gileadites against the men of Ephraim; they fight against them, and kill forty-two thousand Ephraimites at the passages of Jordan, <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.4-Jdg.12.6">Jdg 12:4-6</reference>. Jephthah dies, having judged Israel six years, <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.7">Jdg 12:7</reference>. Ibzan judge seven years, <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.8">Jdg 12:8</reference>. His posterity and death, <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.9">Jdg 12:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.10">Jdg 12:10</reference>. Elon judge ten years, and dies, <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.11">Jdg 12:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.12">Jdg 12:12</reference>. Abdon judge eight years, <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.13">Jdg 12:13</reference>. His posterity and death, <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.14">Jdg 12:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.15">Jdg 12:15</reference>. <div eID="gen8899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8900" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen8900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8901" type="x-p"/> The men of Ephraim gathered themselves together - ויצעק vaiyitstsaek, they called each other to arms; summoning all their tribe and friends to arm themselves to destroy Jephthah and the Gileadites, being jealous lest they should acquire too much power.
entries.2997378d0e52d04203b090409109269270a91bb3: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen8901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8902" type="x-p"/> I put my life in my hands - I exposed myself to the greatest difficulties and dangers. But whence did this form of speech arise? Probably from a man's laying hold of his sword, spear, or bow. "This is the defender of my life; on this, and my proper use of it, my life depends." When a man draws his sword against his foe, his enemy will naturally aim at his life; and his sword in his hand is his sole defense. It is then, Fight and conquer, or die. Thus Jephthah took his life in his hand. This phrase occurs in some other places of Scripture; see <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.5">1Sam 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.21">1Sam 28:21</reference>. And the words of the Conqueror, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">Isa 63:5</reference>, seem to confirm the above view of the subject: I looked, and there was none to help; and I wondered there was none to uphold; therefore mine own arm brought salvation unto me; i.e., by mine own arm I saved my life, and brought destruction on mine enemies.
entries.abdeda0f26b1e0c0b9d3c1c39017d5492b14cd39: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen8902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8903" type="x-p"/> And fought with Ephraim - Some commentators suppose that there were two battles in which the Ephraimites were defeated: the first mentioned in the above clause; and the second occasioned by the taunting language mentioned in the conclusion of the verse, Ye Gileadites are fugitives of Ephraim. Where the point of this reproach lies, or what is the reason of it, cannot be easily ascertained.
entries.7e802a65d4de77ae5c0c3721541d0269fa357caf: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen8903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8904" type="x-p"/> Say now Shibboleth; and he said Sibboleth - The original differs only in the first letter ס samech, instead of ש sheen; אמר נא שבלת ויאמר סבלת emar na Shibboleth, vaiyomer Sibboleth. The difference between ש seen, without a point, which when pointed is pronounced sheen, and ס samech, is supposed by many to be imperceptible. But there can be no doubt there was, to the ears of a Hebrew, a most sensible distinction. Most Europeans, and, indeed, most who have written grammars of the language, perceive scarcely any difference between the Arabic seen and saad; but as both those letters are radical not only in Arabic but in Hebrew, the difference of enunciation must be such as to be plainly perceivable by the ear; else it would be impossible to determine the root of a word into which either of these letters entered, except by guessing, unless by pronunciation the sounds were distinct. One to whom the Arabic is vernacular, hearing a native speak, discerns it in a moment; but the delicate enunciation of the characteristic difference between those letters ש seen and ס samech, and seen and saad, is seldom caught by a European. Had there been no distinction between the seen and samech but what the Masoretic point gives now, then ס samech would not have been used in the word סבלת sibboleth, but ש seen, thus שבלת: but there must have been a very remarkable difference in the pronunciation of the Ephraimites, when instead of שבלת shibboleth, an ear of corn, (see <reference osisRef="Job.24.24">Job 24:24</reference>), they said סבלת sibboleth, which signifies a burden, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.6">Exo 6:6</reference>; and a heavy burden were they obliged to bear who could not pronounce this test letter. It is likely that the Ephraimites were, in reference to the pronunciation of sh, as different from the Gileadites as the people in some parts of the north of England are, in the pronunciation of the letter r, from all the other inhabitants of the land. The sound of th cannot be pronounced by the Persians in general; and yet it is a common sound among the Arabians. To this day multitudes of the German Jews cannot pronounce ת th, but put ss in the stead of it: thus for בית beith (a house) they say bess. Mr. Richardson, in his "Dissertation on the Languages, Literature, and Manners of the Eastern Nations," prefixed to his Persian and Arabic Dictionary, p. ii., 4th. edition, makes some observations on the different dialects which prevailed in Arabia Felix, the chief of which were the Hemyaret and Koreish; and to illustrate the point in hand, he produces the following story from the Mohammedan writers: "An envoy from one of the feudatory states, having been sent to the tobba, (the sovereign), that prince, when he was introduced, pronounced the word T'heb, which in the Hemyaret implied, Be seated: unhappily it signified, in the native dialect of the ambassador, Precipitate thyself; and he, with a singular deference for the orders of his sovereign, threw himself instantly from the castle wall and perished." Though the Ephraimites had not a different dialect, they had, it appears, a different pronunciation, which confounded, to others, letters of the same organ, and thus produced, not only a different sound, but even an opposite meaning. This was a sufficient test to find out an Ephraimite; and he who spake not as he was commanded, at the fords of Jordan, spoke against his own life. <div eID="gen8904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8905" type="x-p"/> For he could not frame to pronounce it right - This is not a bad rendering of the original ולא יכין לדבר כן velo yachin ledabber ken; "and they did not direct to speak it thus." But instead of יכין yachin, to direct, thirteen of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., with two ancient editions, read יבין yabin; "they did not understand to speak it thus." The versions take great latitude in this verse. The Vulgate makes a paraphrase: Dic ergo Shibboleth, quod interpretatur spica: qui respondebat Sibboleth; eadem litera spicam exprimere non valens. "Say therefore, Shibboleth; which interpreted is an ear of corn: but he answered, Sibboleth; not being able to express an ear of corn by that letter." In my very ancient copy of the Vulgate, probably the editio princeps, there is sebboleth in the first instance as the test word, and thebboleth as the Ephraimite pronunciation. But cebboleth is the reading of the Complutensian Polyglot, and is supported by one of my own MSS., yet the former reading, thebboleth, is found in two of my MSS. The Chaldee has שובלתא shubbaltha for the Gileaditish pronunciation, and סבלתא subbaltha for that of Ephraim. The Syriac has shelba and sebla. The Arabic has the same word, with sheen and seen; and adds, "He said Sebla, for the Ephraimites could not pronounce the letter sheen." These notices, however trivial at first view, will not be thought unimportant by the Biblical critic.
entries.fcd742dc91a7cf954bf27a4011a9d481a540c7aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen8905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8906" type="x-p"/> And after him Ibzan - It appears that during the administration of Jephthah, six years - Ibzan, seven years - Elon, ten years - and Abdon, eight years, (in the whole thirty-one years), the Israelites had peace in all their borders; and we shall find by the following chapter that in this time of rest they corrupted themselves, and were afterwards delivered into the power of the Philistines. <div eID="gen8906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8907" type="x-p"/> 1. We find that Ibzan had a numerous family, sixty children; and Abdon had forty sons and thirty grandsons; and that they lived splendidly, which is here expressed by their riding on seventy young asses; what we would express by they all kept their carriages; for the riding on fine asses in those days was not less dignified than riding in coaches in ours. <div eID="gen8907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8908" type="x-p"/> 2. It does not appear that any thing particular took place in the civil state of the Israelites during the time of these latter judges; nothing is said concerning their administration, whether it was good or bad; nor is any thing mentioned of the state of religion. It is likely that they enjoyed peace without, and their judges were capable of preventing discord and sedition within. Yet, doubtless, God was at work among them, though there were none to record the operations either of his hand or his Spirit; but the people who feared him no doubt bore testimony to the word of his grace.  <chapter eID="Judg.12"/> <div eID="gen8908" type="x-p"/>

entries.12697001144df1eb9271d478216668231b2e8190: Jdg 12:1-3 <div eID="gen3374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3375" type="x-p"/> Jephthah’s War with the Ephraimites, and Office of Judge. - Jdg 12:1. The jealousy of the tribe of Ephraim, which was striving after the leadership, had already shown itself in the time of Gideon in such a way that nothing but the moderation of that judge averted open hostilities. And now that the tribes on the east of the Jordan had conquered the Ammonites under the command of Jephthah without the co-operation of the Ephraimites, Ephraim thought it necessary to assert its claim to take the lead in Israel in a very forcible manner. The Ephraimites gathered themselves together, and went over צפונה. This is generally regarded as an appellative noun (<hi type="italic">northward</hi>); but in all probability it is a proper name, “to <hi type="italic">Zaphon</hi>,” the city of the Gadites in the Jordan valley, which is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.27">Jos 13:27</reference> along with Succoth, that is to say, according to a statement of the <hi type="italic">Gemara</hi>, though of a very uncertain character no doubt, Ἀμαθοῦς (<hi type="italic">Joseph</hi>. Ant. xiii. 13, 5, xiv. 5, 4; Bell. Judg. i. 4, 2, <hi type="italic">Reland</hi>, Pal. pp. 308 and 559-60), the modern ruins of <hi type="italic">Amata</hi> on the Wady <hi type="italic">Rajîb</hi> or <hi type="italic">Ajlun</hi>, the situation of which would suit this passage very well. They then threatened Jephthah, because he had made war upon the Ammonites without them, and said, “<hi type="italic">We will burn thy house over thee with fire.</hi>” Their arrogance and threat Jephthah opposed most energetically. He replied (Jdg 12:2, Jdg 12:3), “<hi type="italic">A man of strife have I been, I and my people on the one hand, and the children of Ammon on the other, very greatly,</hi>” i.e., I and my people had a severe conflict with the Ammonites. “<hi type="italic">Then I called you, but ye did not deliver me out of their hand; and when I saw that thou </hi>(Ephraim) <hi type="italic">didst not help me, I put my life in my hand</hi>” (i.e., I risked my own life: see <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.5">1Sa 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.21">1Sa 28:21</reference>; Job 13:14. The <hi type="italic">Kethibh</hi> אישׂמה comes from ישׂם: cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.24.33">Gen 24:33</reference>), “<hi type="italic">and I went against the Ammonites, and Jehovah gave them into my hand.</hi>” Jephthah’s appeal to the Ephraimites to fight against the Ammonites it not mentioned in Judg 11, probably for no other reason than because it was without effect. The Ephraimites, however, had very likely refused their co-operation simply because the Gileadites had appointed Jephthah as commander without consulting them. Consequently the Ephraimites had no ground whatever for rising up against Jephthah and the Gileadites in this haughty and hostile manner; and Jephthah had a perfect right not only to ask them, “<hi type="italic">Wherefore are ye come up against me now</hi> (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. 'this day'), to <hi type="italic">fight against me?</hi>” but to resist such conduct with the sword.
entries.b62e965ec6a27d10a9d0e6505117459e4a91d234: Jdg 12:4 <div eID="gen3375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3376" type="x-p"/> He therefore gathered together all the men (men of war) of Gilead and smote the Ephraimites, because they had said, “<hi type="italic">Ye Gileadites are fugitives of Ephraim in the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh.</hi>” The meaning of these obscure words is probably the following: Ye Gileadites are a mob gathered together from Ephraimites that have run away; “ye are an obscure set of men, men of no name, dwelling in the midst of two most noble and illustrious tribes” (<hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>). This contemptuous speech did not apply to the tribes of Reuben and Gad as such, but simply to the warriors whom Jephthah had gathered together out of Gilead. For the words are not to be rendered <hi type="italic">erepti Ephraim,</hi> “the rescued of Ephraim,” as they are by <hi type="italic">Seb</hi>. <hi type="italic">Schmidt</hi> and <hi type="italic">Stud</hi>., or to be understood as referring to the fact that the Gileadites had found refuge with the Ephraimites during the eighteen years of oppression on the part of the Ammonites, since such an explanation is at variance with the use of the word פּליט, which simply denotes a fugitive who has escaped from danger, and not one who has sought and found protection with another. The Ephraimites had to pay for this insult offered to their brethren by a terrible defeat.
entries.d064f438a92b7947b7c158b045e74fad96b7b858: Jdg 12:5-6 <div eID="gen3376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3377" type="x-p"/> When the Gileadites had beaten the Ephraimites, they took the fords of the Jordan before the Ephraimites (or towards Ephraim: see Jdg 3:28; Jdg 7:24), to cut off their retreat and prevent their return to their homes. And “<hi type="italic">when fugitives of Ephraim wanted to cross, the men of Gilead asked them, Art thou Ephrathi,</hi>” i.e., an Ephraimite? <hi type="italic">And if he said no,</hi> they made him pronounce the word <hi type="italic">Shibboleth</hi> (a stream or flood, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.3">Psa 69:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.16">Psa 69:16</reference>; not an ear of corn, which is quite unsuitable here); “<hi type="italic">and if he said, Sibboleth, not taking care to pronounce it correctly, they laid hold of him and put him to death at the fords of the Jordan.</hi>” In this manner there fell at that time, i.e., during the whole war, 42,000 Ephraimites. The “<hi type="italic">fugitives of Ephraim</hi>” were the Ephraimites who had escaped from the battle and wished to return home. The expression is used here in its ordinary sense, and not with the contemptuous sense in which the Ephraimites had used it in Jdg 12:4. From this history we learn quite casually that the Ephraimites generally pronounced <hi type="italic">sh</hi> (shin) like <hi type="italic">s</hi> (samech). הכין is used elliptically for לב הכין, to direct his heart to anything, pay heed (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.22">1Sa 23:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.2">1Ch 28:2</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.14">2Ch 12:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.19">2Ch 30:19</reference>).
entries.174e650fe317622e3313d569dd756931521fc232: Jdg 12:7 <div eID="gen3377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3378" type="x-p"/> Jephthah judged Israel six years, though most probably only the tribes on the east of the Jordan. When he died, he was buried in one of the towns of Gilead. The plural גלעד בּערי is used quite indefinitely, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.13.12">Gen 13:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.6.2">Neh 6:2</reference>, etc. (see <hi type="italic">Ges</hi>. Lehrgeb. p. 665), simply because the historian did not know the exact town.
entries.f98d4242026b6b389fe8a449dbd63570094450f0: Jdg 12:8-15 <div eID="gen3378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3379" type="x-p"/> Of these three judges no particular deeds are related, just as in the case of Tola and Jair (see the remarks on Jdg 10:1). But it certainly follows from the expression אחריו ויּשׁפּט (Jdg 12:8, Jdg 12:11, Jdg 12:13) that they were one after another successors of Jephthah, and therefore that their office of judge also extended simply over the tribes on the east of the Jordan, and perhaps the northern tribes on this side.  Jdg 12:8-10 <hi type="italic">Ibzan</hi> sprang from <hi type="italic">Bethlehem</hi>,-hardly, however, the town of that name in the tribe of Judah, as <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> affirms (Ant. v. 7, 13), for that is generally distinguished either as Bethlehem “of Judah” (Jdg 17:7, Jdg 17:9; Rth 1:2; <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.12">1Sa 17:12</reference>), or Bethlehem <hi type="italic">Ephratah</hi> (Mic 5:1), but probably Bethlehem in the tribe of Zebulun (<reference osisRef="Josh.9.15">Jos 9:15</reference>). He had thirty sons and thirty daughters, the latter of whom he sent away החוּצה (out of his house), i.e., gave them in marriage, and brought home thirty women in their places from abroad as wives for his sons. He judged Israel seven years, and was buried in Bethlehem.

entries.102993a614ee2116d3d630a76fe11ad96a30cb0a:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="12" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>AND the men of Ephraim <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> called.</ns0:note> gathered them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves together, and went northward <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Over <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> so Northward towards <ns0:hi>Mizpeh,</ns0:hi> where <ns0:hi>Iepthah</ns0:hi> was, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 11. 34. and which was in the Northern part of the Land beyond <ns0:hi>Iordan.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and said unto Jephthah <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Through Pride and Envy, conrending with him, as they did before with <ns0:hi>Gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deon, Iudg.</ns0:hi> 8. 1.</ns0:note>, Wherefore passedst thou over <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Not over <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> for there he was al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ready; but over the Borders of the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> land beyond <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> as appears by comparing this with <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 11. 29. where the same Phrase is used.</ns0:note> to fight against the children of Ammon, and didst not call us to go with thee? We will burn thine house upon thee with fire.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And Jephthah said unto them, I and my peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple were at great strife with the children of Am<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon; and when I called you <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Hence it appears, that he craved their assistance, which they denied; though that be not elsewhere ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressed.</ns0:note>, ye delivered me not out of their hand.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And when I saw that ye delivered <ns0:hi>me</ns0:hi> not, I put my life in my hand <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> I exposed my self to utmost danger<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> as a man that carries a brittle and precious thing in his hand, which may easily either fall to the ground, or be snatch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed from him. The same Phrase is used 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19. 5. and 28. 21. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 13. 14. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 119. 109.</ns0:note>, and passed over against the children of Ammon, and the LORD deliver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed them into my hand. Wherefore then are ye come up unto me this day to fight against me <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Why do you thus requite my kindness in running into such ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />zard to preserve you and yours?</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Then Jephthah gathered together all the men of Gilead, and fought with Ephraim: and the men of Gilead smote Ephraim, because they said<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Ye Gileadites <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> fugitives of Ephraim, among the Ephraimites, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> among the Manassites <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">According to this Translation, these words are a scoffing and contemptuous expression of the <ns0:hi>Ephraimites</ns0:hi> concerning the <ns0:hi>Gileadites,</ns0:hi> whom they call Fugitives of <ns0:hi>Ephraim;</ns0:hi> the word <ns0:hi>Ephraim</ns0:hi> being here taken largely, as it is elsewhere, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 7. 2, 5. so as it comprehends the other Neighbouring Tribes, of which <ns0:hi>Ephraim</ns0:hi> was in some sort the head or chief; and especially their Brethren of <ns0:hi>Manasseh,</ns0:hi> who lived next to them, and were descended from the same Father, <ns0:hi>Ioseph;</ns0:hi> by reason whereof, both these Tribes are sometimes reckoned for one, and called by the name of <ns0:hi>the Tribe of Ioseph.</ns0:hi> And this large signification of <ns0:hi>Ephraim</ns0:hi> may seem probable from the following words, where instead of <ns0:hi>Ephraim</ns0:hi> is put <ns0:hi>the Ephraimites, and the Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nassites.</ns0:hi> By <ns0:hi>Gileadites</ns0:hi> here they seem principally to mean the <ns0:hi>Manassites</ns0:hi> beyond <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> who dwelt in <ns0:hi>Gilead,</ns0:hi> as ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pears from <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 3. 13. <ns0:hi>Iosh.</ns0:hi> 17. 1, 5, 6. And although other <ns0:hi>Gileadites</ns0:hi> were joyn'd with them, yet they vent their passion against these; principally, because they envied them most; partly, because they seem to have had a chief hand in the Victory, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 11. 29. And partly, because they were more nearly related to them, and therefore more obliged to de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sire their Conjunction with them in the War. These they here opprobriously call <ns0:hi>fugitives, i. e.</ns0:hi> such as had deserted their Brethren of <ns0:hi>Ephraim</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Manasseh,</ns0:hi> and for some worldly advantage planted themselves beyond <ns0:hi>Iordan</ns0:hi> at a distance from their Brethren, and were alienated in Affecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on from them, and carried on a distinct and separate Inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est of their own; as appears by their Monopolizing the glory of this Success to themselves, and excluding their Bre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thren from it. According to the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> the words lie, and may be rendred thus, <ns0:hi>Therefore</ns0:hi> (so <ns0:hi>chi</ns0:hi> is oft rendred) <ns0:hi>they said, Fugitives of Ephraim are ye; (i. e.</ns0:hi> Ye <ns0:hi>Ephraimites</ns0:hi> are meer run-aways: for the words next foregoing are, <ns0:hi>the men of Gilead smote Ephraim.</ns0:hi> And having told you what they said, because the Pronoun <ns0:hi>they</ns0:hi> was ambiguous, he adds by way of Explication) who said it, even, the <ns0:hi>Gileadites</ns0:hi> (and they said it when they had got the advantage over them, and got between them and home, as the next verse shews) be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing <ns0:hi>between Ephraim and Manasseh; i. e.</ns0:hi> Having taken the passages of <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> as it follows, which lay between <ns0:hi>Ephraim</ns0:hi> and that part of <ns0:hi>Manasseh</ns0:hi> which was beyond <ns0:hi>Iordan.</ns0:hi> Or these latter words may be rendred thus, And <ns0:hi>the Gileadites</ns0:hi> were <ns0:hi>between Ephraim and Manasseh.</ns0:hi> So there is only an <ns0:hi>Ellipsis</ns0:hi> of two small words, which are oft defective, and to be understood in Scripture. Or thus, And <ns0:hi>the Gileadites</ns0:hi> were <ns0:hi>in the midst of the Ephraimites,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>in the midst of the Manassites,</ns0:hi> to wit, those <ns0:hi>Manassites</ns0:hi> who ordinarily lived within <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> who possibly were confederate with the <ns0:hi>Ephra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />imites</ns0:hi> in this quarrel. And so the meaning is, they followed close after them, and overtook them, and fell upon the midst of them, and smote them; and they sent a party to intercept them at the passages of <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> as it here follows.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:203" />5 And the Gileadites took the passages of Jor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dan before the Ephraimites: and it was <ns0:hi>so,</ns0:hi> that when those Ephraimites which were escaped <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>The fugitives of Ephraim,</ns0:hi> as before; for the Hebrew words are the same. Which may make the latter Expositi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of the foregoing words more probable, to wit, that it is not the <ns0:hi>Gileadites,</ns0:hi> but the <ns0:hi>Ephraimites</ns0:hi> who are there as well as here so called, because they were smitten before <ns0:hi>Iep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thah,</ns0:hi> and fled from him.</ns0:note>, said, Let me go over, that the men of Gilead said unto him, <ns0:hi>Art</ns0:hi> thou an Ephraimite? If he said, Nay <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To avoid the present danger.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Then said they unto him, Say now Shibbo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />leth <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Which signifies <ns0:hi>a stream</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>river,</ns0:hi> which they desired to pass over: so it was a word proper for the occasion, and gave them no cause to suspect the Design, because they were required onely to express their desire, to go over the <ns0:hi>Shib<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />boleth</ns0:hi> or River.</ns0:note>; and he said, Sibboleth <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">It is well known, that not only divers Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions, but divers Provinces, or parts of the same Nation who use the same Language, differ in their dialect and man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner of pronunciation.</ns0:note>: for he could not frame to pronounce <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> right <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or rather, <ns0:hi>he did not frame</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>direct</ns0:hi> himself <ns0:hi>to speak so,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>to speak right; i. e.</ns0:hi> So as he was required to do it. The Hebrew Text doth not say that <ns0:hi>he could not</ns0:hi> do it, but that he <ns0:hi>did</ns0:hi> it <ns0:hi>not,</ns0:hi> because he suspect<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing not the design of it, uttered it speedily according to his manner of Expression.</ns0:note>. Then they took him, and slew him at the passages of Jordan: and there fell at that time <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not in that place, at the passages of <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> but in that Expedition, being slain either in the Battel, or in the Pursuit, or at <ns0:hi>Iordan.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> of the Ephraimites forty and two thousand.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And Jephthah judged Israel six years: then died Jephthah the Gileadite, and was buried in <ns0:hi>one of</ns0:hi> the cities <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>In the cities.</ns0:hi> The Plural Number put for the Sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gular, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 19. 29. where <ns0:hi>Lot</ns0:hi> is said to dwell <ns0:hi>in the cities, i. e.</ns0:hi> one of the Cities: And 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 18. 21<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>the twain</ns0:hi> is put for <ns0:hi>one of the twain:</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 18. 14. <ns0:hi>Houses</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>house:</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> 1. 5. <ns0:hi>The sides,</ns0:hi> for one of the sides.</ns0:note> of Gilead.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 ¶ And after him Ibzan of Bethlehem <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Either that in <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> of which <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 2. 6. Or that in <ns0:hi>Zebulun, Iosh.</ns0:hi> 19. 15.</ns0:note> judged Israel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And he had thirty sons, and thirty daughters, <ns0:hi>whom</ns0:hi> he had sent abroad, and took <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Took them home for Wives to hip Sons. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 24. 67. and 31. 50. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 21. 12. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 11. 27.</ns0:note> in thirty daughters from abroad for his sons. And he judged Israel seven years.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Then died Ibzan, and was buried at Beth<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lehem.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And after him, Elon a Zebulonite judged Israel; and he judged Israel ten years.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And Elon the Zebulonite died, and was bu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ried in Ajelon, in the country of Zebulun <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">This is added to distinguish it from other <ns0:hi>Asalons,</ns0:hi> of which see <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 1. 35. 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 6. 69. and 8. 13.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 ¶ And after him, Abdon the son of Hillel a Pirathonite judged Israel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And he had forty sons, and thirty <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Sons sons.</ns0:note> ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phews, that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 5. 10. and 10. 4.</ns0:note> rode on threescore and ten ass colts, and he judged Israel eight years.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And Abdon the son of Hillel the Piratho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nite died, and was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the mount of the Amalekites <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">So called from some remarkable Exploit, done either by, or upon the <ns0:hi>Amalekites</ns0:hi> in that place.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
